explain.say: Your phone wants 5 volts, but a car socket gives 12. Burn off the extra 7 volts in a resistor and you waste more than half the power. The buck converter does the job almost loss-free with a switch, an inductor and a capacitor. On the board is the converter with its switch on: 12 volts in, and a 2.5 ohm load that wants 5 volts and 2 amps.

explain.say: Look at the voltage just after the switch. The MOSFET, a fast transistor switch, flicks on and off 100,000 times a second. On for 4.17 microseconds, the switch node sits at 12 volts; off for the rest of each 10 microsecond period, it is near 0. The fraction of time on is the duty cycle, D, here 0.417. What is the average of that square wave?

explain.say: Five volts, just what we want. But the load needs smooth DC, not pulses. The inductor smooths the current: while the switch is on, its current ramps up; when it is off, a diode gives it a path and it ramps down. See the triangle between 1.69 and 2.31 amps, centred on the 2 amp load. Why doesn't the current stop when the switch opens?

Because an inductor fights any change in its current, so it keeps pushing, drawing through the diode. The capacitor irons out what is left of the ripple. Now the beauty: an ideal buck wastes nothing, so 10 watts out means 10 watts in, only 0.83 amps from the 12 volt source. Voltage went down and current went up, like a DC transformer. What does a real one lose?

faq.q: How does a buck converter work?
faq.a: A transistor switch chops the input voltage into fast pulses, and an inductor and capacitor average them into smooth DC. The output voltage equals the duty cycle times the input voltage, so 42 percent on-time turns 12 volts into 5.
asks: What is a step-down DC-DC converter?

faq.q: How do you calculate the duty cycle of a buck converter?
faq.a: For an ideal buck in continuous conduction, D equals V out over V in. For 5 volts from 12 volts, D is 5 over 12, about 0.417, or 41.7 percent.
asks: What is the buck converter formula?

faq.q: What does the inductor do in a buck converter?
faq.a: It stores energy while the switch is on and releases it while the switch is off, keeping the load current flowing smoothly. Its current ramps up and down in a small triangle around the average load current.
asks: Why does a buck converter need an inductor?

faq.q: Why is a buck converter more efficient than a linear regulator?
faq.a: A linear regulator drops the extra voltage across a transistor and burns it as heat, so going from 12 to 5 volts can never beat 42 percent. A buck switch is either fully on or fully off, so it wastes very little, typically reaching 90 percent or more.

Ripple equals input minus output voltage, times the duty cycle, divided by inductance times switching frequency. With 7 volts, 0.417, 47 microhenries and 100 kilohertz, it is about 0.62 amps peak to peak; a bigger inductor or a higher frequency makes it smaller.
asks: How do you calculate inductor ripple?

facts: An ideal buck converter's output is Vout = D × Vin.
A linear regulator dropping 12 V to 5 V can never be more than about 42% efficient.
